definitions.definition: Torus=reals/(2*pi*integers), with normalized measure dx/(2*pi). Periodic spatial products, integrals and derivatives are on this torus. A trigonometric polynomial is a finite sum of exp(i*k*x) with integer k.

For a periodic integrable f, hat f(k)=(2*pi)^(-1) integral_0^(2*pi) f(x)exp(-i*k*x) dx, k in Z. Extend Fourier coefficients to periodic distributions. Reality means hat f(-k)=conjugate(hat f(k)); mean zero means hat f(0)=0. For sequences, ell^2 is the square-summable sequence space with counting measure.

definitions.type: family of real or complex Hilbert spaces indexed by real order
definitions.definition: Write <k>=(1+k^2)^(1/2). H^s is the completion of trigonometric polynomials with ||f||_(H^s)^2=sum_{k in Z}<k>^(2s)|hat f(k)|^2, interpreted as distributions for s<0. L^2=H^0 and ||.||_2 denotes its normalized norm. For mean-zero f, ||f||_(dot H^s)^2=sum_{k!=0}|k|^(2s)|hat f(k)|^2. For s>=0, ||f||_(dot H^s)<=||f||_(H^s)<=2^(s/2)||f||_(dot H^s); for s<0, 2^(s/2)||f||_(dot H^s)<=||f||_(H^s)<=||f||_(dot H^s). In time L^infty norms are essential suprema, replaced by ordinary suprema for continuous representatives; derivative norms remain essential suprema.

definitions.type: one-parameter family of linear Fourier operators
definitions.definition: For real t, S_t=exp(-t*partial_x^3) has Fourier multiplier exp(i*t*k^3).
Dinv=partial_x^(-1) has multiplier (i*k)^(-1) for k!=0 and zero at zero. Write Dinv2=(Dinv)^2=partial_x^(-2). Spatial differentiation partial_x has multiplier i*k.
B_t(f,g)=S_(-t) partial_x[(S_t f)(S_t g)]. Initially use smooth inputs; the negative Sobolev extension to L^2 inputs is proved below.

definitions.type: distributional evolution equation and smooth-approximation solution convention
definitions.definition: KdV is u_t+u_xxx=(1/2)partial_x(u^2), u(0)=u0, with real mean-zero data on Torus. An exact solution at regularity sigma>=0 means its unique real mean-zero C([0,T];H^sigma) distributional solution obtained as the limit of smooth-data solutions. This convention alone grants neither existence nor a bound; these are proved from the registered flow source. For an existing solution write its twisted path v(t)=S_(-t)u(t).

inputs.statement: Source flow assertions on the normalized 2*pi torus, in mean-zero homogeneous spaces: for real mean-zero initial datum q, define U_t=U*U_x+U_xxx and its twist y_k(t)=exp(i*t*k^3)hat U(t,k), satisfying y'_k=(i*k/2)sum_{r+s=k}exp(3*i*k*r*s*t)y_r*y_s. (i) For sigma>=0, horizon b>0, and ||q||_2<=B0, the Galerkin approximations with nonlinearity projected onto |k|<=m are uniformly bounded in L^infty([0,b];dot H^sigma) by A_sigma depending only on sigma,b,B0,||q||_(dot H^sigma). (ii) If sigma>0 and 0<rho<sigma, a subsequence converges strongly in L^p([0,b];H^rho), every fixed 1<p<infinity, and weak-* in L^infty dot H^sigma to a coefficientwise integral solution with the same bound and ||y(t)||_2=||q||_2 a.e.. (iii) That solution is unique, is in C([0,b];dot H^sigma), conserves L^2 for every time, and depends Lipschitz continuously on initial data in dot H^sigma: for sigma>1/2 the constant may depend on sigma,b and the two initial dot H^sigma norms; for 0<sigma<=1/2 the continuity and uniqueness assertions hold with the same indicated topology. For sigma=0 there is a unique C([0,b];dot H^0) solution obtained by smooth approximation, Lipschitz in its data. (iv) For -1<theta<=0, any two such flows whose initial L^2 norms sum to at most B0 satisfy sup_[0,b]||y-z||_(dot H^theta)<=C'(B0,theta)*C_(B0,theta)^b*||y(0)-z(0)||_(dot H^theta). The same norm statements hold for U by the Fourier twist.
source_conditions: The source data are real and mean-zero on the 2*pi torus, and the horizon b is positive.
The Sobolev orders in (i)-(iii) satisfy the indicated nonnegative or positive ranges, and the initial homogeneous norms are finite.
For (i) the initial L^2 norm is bounded by B0; for (iv) the sum of the two initial L^2 norms is at most B0 and -1<theta<=0.

output.statement: For every real mean-zero q in H^gamma with ||q||_(H^gamma)<=R, KdV has the exact solution prescribed in D020; it belongs to C([0,T];H^gamma), and sup_[0,T]||u(t)||_(H^gamma)<=A(T,gamma,R)<infinity uniformly in q. For smooth q the solution is smooth. The twist v=S_(-t)u has the same norms and satisfies v'=B_t(v,v)/2. For any two such solutions with initial L^2 norms summing to at most B0, sup_[0,T]||u-Utilde||_2<=C(T,B0)||q-qtilde||_2. In particular smooth approximations with bounded H^gamma norm converge in C([0,T];L^2); M=1+sup_[0,T]||v||_(H^gamma) is bounded by 1+A(T,gamma,R).

argument.text: Fix an arbitrary datum q and assume L1: q is real and mean-zero, belongs to H^gamma, and ||q||_(H^gamma)<=R. H001-H003 give T>0, 0<gamma<=1, R>0. Reflection with a minus sign sends q to -q(-x) without changing any Fourier Sobolev norm. Apply E001's positive-regularity existence and uniqueness clauses at sigma=gamma, horizon T, and initial L^2 bound R; at smooth data apply them at every higher order as well, and uniqueness identifies these solutions. Its homogeneous bounds transfer to the inhomogeneous norms because 1<=<k>/|k|<=sqrt(2) for k!=0. Thus the source solutions have a common H^gamma bound depending only on T,gamma,R. E001's bound can equivalently be taken uniformly on the initial norm ball as stated in its bound clause.

produces.statement: The source flow for -q(-x) exists, is unique and continuous at order gamma, and has an H^gamma bound A(T,gamma,R); smooth q gives smooth flow.

argument.text: Set u(t,x)=-U(t,-x). At (t,-x), u_t=-U_t, u_x=U_x and u_xxx=U_xxx, so u_t+u_xxx=-U*U_x=u*u_x. Also hat u(k)=-hat U(-k), preserving reality, mean and all norms. The initial datum is q. Reflection is an involution, so source uniqueness transfers. The source coefficientwise integrated equation becomes distributional KdV under this change: products of L^2 functions are L^1, and each tested Fourier coefficient is absolutely integrable in time. Twisting by S_(-t) removes the linear term and gives v'=B_t(v,v)/2. Unitarity follows directly from the modulus-one multiplier; hence M=1+sup||v||_(H^gamma)<=1+A(T,gamma,R).

produces.statement: u is the unique real mean-zero C([0,T];H^gamma) distributional KdV solution with datum q, v=S_(-t)u satisfies v'=B_t(v,v)/2, and sup||u||_(H^gamma)<=A(T,gamma,R). For smooth q, u is smooth.

argument.text: For any two such initial data with L^2 norms summing to B0 or less, apply E001(iv) at theta=0 and horizon T to their reflected data. Twisting and reflection preserve the L^2 distance, giving sup||u-Utilde||_2<=C(T,B0)||q-qtilde||_2. In particular the real mean-zero Fourier truncations of q converge to q in H^gamma and L^2, stay in the same norm ball, and their flows converge uniformly in L^2; uniqueness identifies the limit with the flow just constructed. Thus this is exactly the prescribed smooth-approximation solution. The uniform H^gamma bound also passes to the limit by taking limits in every finite nonnegative Fourier norm sum and then their supremum. Discharge L1 and quantify q and the two-flow assertion; this proves every clause of the asserted conclusion.

The initial L^2 norm is <=R by L1; the two-flow clause is not used in this application.

Smooth q has a finite homogeneous norm at every chosen sigma>gamma>0, so the positive-regularity existence and uniqueness clauses apply.
Its initial L^2 norm is <=R by L1; clause(iv) is not used here.
